newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Conviction likely to cost Malaysian opposition MP his seat.
newsitem.headline: Conviction likely to cost Malaysian opposition MP his seat.

text.p: A leading Malaysian opposition politician was found guilty on Monday of sedition and faces the loss of his parliamentary seat in a case that has drawn international attention.
The High Court in west coast Malacca state found Lim Guan Eng, youth leader of the Democratic Action Party (DAP), guilty on two charges of sedition and spreading false news.
He was fined 15,000 ringgit ($5,976) for violating the Sedition Act and the Printing and Publications Act.

Under article 48 of the Federal Constitution, a member of parliament is disqualified if he is sentenced to a year's jail or a 2,000 ringgit ($800) fine. The disqualification takes effect 14 days from the day of conviction, barring an appeal.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International said in a recent statement the charges were "politically motivated, designed to intimidate dissenting voices and to limit debate on an issue of public concern".
Lim was charged with making false statements in 1995 about Malacca's Chief Minister Rahim Tamby Chik, who was accused by a then 15-year-old schoolgirl of having an affair with her.
Rahim, who at the time was a rising star in Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) as head of that party's youth wing, denied the accusation.
The attorney-general said at the time that there was insufficient evidence to bring charges, but Rahim was forced to quit his party and state posts over the scandal.
Lim said the girl, kept in police custody for more than a week for investigation of the complaint, was an "imprisoned victim" in the case and Rahim should be in jail instead.
The prosecution contended the statement was seditious because it seemed to accuse police of illegally detaining the girl.
Lim said he would file an appeal "but the severity of the sentence does not leave much room for optimism".

The sentence was "disappointing in the sense that I will be disqualified as a member of parliament, despite being elected consecutively for three terms", Lim told reporters after the verdict. "My constituents have been denied my services."
The case "will create a sense of fear and intimidation among those who wish to support the struggle for greater democratisation or more respect for human rights", he said.
The opposition holds 30 seats in the 192-seat parliament. The DAP with nine seats is the largest opposition party.
But in his judgement, High Court Justice Mohamed Noor said he did not think Lim should be diqualified from parliament.
"I have also considered article 48 in this case and feel it is wrong to mete out a punishment to prevent a person from losing his eligibility to be a Member of Parliament," he said.
Lim Kit Siang, Lim's father and the opposition leader in parliament, said he was not surprised by the verdict.
"What is a matter of concern to all Malaysians is that this is another example of selected prosecution," he told reporters at the courthouse.
"If every political leader is to be prosecuted for false news, I don't think there will be a single cabinet minister in Malaysia," the elder Lim said.
The Attorney-General's office was not available for comment on the elder Lim's statements.
Both father and son were detained from 1987 to 1989 under Malaysia's Internal Security Act, which allows almost indefinite detention without charges or trial.
